claims.text: The low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi result partly from low intrinsic lattice friction.
Efficient dynamic recovery contributes to the alloy's low hardness and strength.
Dislocation cross-slip and climb cause rapid dislocation annihilation rather than accumulation during deformation.
The applicable initial state is a homogeneous, single-phase CoCrFeNiTi solid solution.
The applicable initial state has a fine and uniform grain structure.
Changing strain rate and temperature modulates the balance between dislocation multiplication and recovery.
Low lattice friction permits dislocations to glide easily.
Dynamic recovery reduces dislocation density by eliminating dislocations.
Dynamic recovery prevents the dislocation buildup required for substantial work hardening.
Limited work hardening produces low hardness and strength while retaining good plasticity and machinability.
High strain rate or low temperature suppresses dynamic recovery relative to elevated-temperature or low-strain-rate deformation.
Suppressing dynamic recovery will increase the post-deformation dislocation density.
The increased dislocation density produced under recovery-suppressing conditions will enhance strain hardening.
Recovery-suppressing conditions will produce higher measured hardness and strength than recovery-favoring conditions.
Room-temperature deformation of the starting alloy exhibits high plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength.
Dynamic recovery is active during the proposed room-temperature baseline tests.
The hypothesis is restricted to equimolar CoCrFeNiTi without secondary phases or ordering.
Secondary phases, ordering, or extreme deformation conditions may activate mechanisms outside the proposed recovery-controlled explanation.
